blocks.body:
In the 1920s Hilbert proposed a programme: write down a mechanically checkable list of axioms from which every true statement of arithmetic could be proved, and prove by elementary means that these axioms never lead to a contradiction. In 1931 Gödel showed that neither half can be achieved. Any consistent axiom system that is listed by a mechanical rule and can do a modest amount of arithmetic leaves some arithmetical sentence undecided: it proves neither the sentence nor its negation. And such a system cannot prove its own consistency.

These are theorems about formal systems, proved with the same rigour as any theorem about primes. This page states them precisely, explains the two key tools (coding syntax by numbers, and self-reference by diagonalisation), proves the first theorem, sketches the second, and connects both to the undecidability of the halting problem. It assumes the [[completeness-theorem]] page and basic [[computability]].

blocks.title: Theories and their properties
Coding syntax by numbers
blocks.body:
Gödel's first idea is that formulas and proofs, being finite strings, can be coded as natural numbers, so that statements about provability become statements about numbers. Give each symbol a code number. A string with symbol codes $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_k$ gets the Gödel number
$$2^{a_1} \cdot 3^{a_2} \cdot 5^{a_3} \cdots p_k^{a_k},$$
where $p_k$ is the $k$-th prime. By unique factorisation ([[fta]]) the string can be recovered from its number. A proof, being a finite sequence of formulas, is coded the same way from the codes of its lines. Write $\ulcorner \sigma \urcorner$ for the numeral (the term $SS\cdots S0$) of the Gödel number of $\sigma$.

The point of the coding is that the syntactic operations become computable functions of numbers: whether $n$ codes a formula, whether $n$ codes an axiom of $T$ (this is where effective axiomatisation is used), and whether $m$ codes a deduction whose last line is coded by $n$. Every computable relation of numbers is representable in $Q$: there is a formula $\mathrm{Prf}_T(y, x)$ such that whenever $m$ codes a proof of the sentence coded by $n$, $Q \vdash \mathrm{Prf}_T(\underline{m}, \underline{n})$, and whenever it does not, $Q \vdash \neg\mathrm{Prf}_T(\underline{m}, \underline{n})$, where $\underline m$ is the numeral of $m$. This is a long but routine verification, which we take for granted. Define
$$\mathrm{Prov}_T(x) \;=\; \exists y\, \mathrm{Prf}_T(y, x),$$
"$x$ is the code of a theorem of $T$".

blocks.title: Diagonal lemma
blocks.body:
Let $T$ extend $Q$. For every formula $\varphi(x)$ with one free variable there is a sentence $\sigma$ such that
$$T \vdash \sigma \leftrightarrow \varphi(\ulcorner \sigma \urcorner).$$

blocks.title: Proof sketch
blocks.body: The function $d$ that sends the code of a formula $\psi(x)$ to the code of the sentence $\psi(\ulcorner \psi \urcorner)$, the formula applied to its own code, is computable, so it is representable by a formula $D(x, y)$, with $Q$ proving that $D(\ulcorner\psi\urcorner, y)$ holds for exactly one $y$, namely the code of $\psi(\ulcorner\psi\urcorner)$. Let $\psi(x) = \exists y\, (D(x,y) \wedge \varphi(y))$, "the diagonal of $x$ has property $\varphi$", and let $\sigma = \psi(\ulcorner \psi \urcorner)$. Then $\sigma$ says that the diagonal of $\psi$, which is $\sigma$ itself, has property $\varphi$, and the representability of $d$ turns this into a proof of $\sigma \leftrightarrow \varphi(\ulcorner\sigma\urcorner)$ in $T$. The same trick makes a computer program print its own source code.

blocks.title: First incompleteness theorem
blocks.body:
Let $T$ be a consistent, effectively axiomatised theory in the language of arithmetic that extends $Q$. Then there is a sentence $G$ such that $T 
vdash G$ and $T 
vdash 
eg G$. So $T$ is incomplete.

(Gödel's original proof assumed that $T$ is $\omega$-consistent, a little more than consistent; Rosser (1936) showed plain consistency is enough. Below we prove the version in which $T$ is also sound, which already covers PA.)

blocks.title: Proof for sound theories
blocks.body:
Apply the diagonal lemma to $
eg \mathrm{Prov}_T(x)$: there is $G$ with
$$T \vdash G \leftrightarrow 
eg \mathrm{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G \urcorner).$$
Read in $\mathbb N$, $G$ says "I am not a theorem of $T$."

Suppose $T \vdash G$. Then some number $m$ codes a proof of $G$, so $Q \vdash \mathrm{Prf}_T(\underline m, \ulcorner G \urcorner)$, hence $T \vdash \mathrm{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G \urcorner)$. By the displayed equivalence, $T \vdash 
eg G$ as well, and $T$ is inconsistent. So $T 
vdash G$.

Since $G$ is not a theorem, no number codes a proof of it, so $
eg \mathrm{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G \urcorner)$ is true in $\mathbb N$; as $T$ is sound, the provable equivalence $G \leftrightarrow 
eg \mathrm{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G \urcorner)$ is true in $\mathbb N$ too, so $G$ is true in $\mathbb N$. Then $
eg G$ is false in $\mathbb N$, and a sound $T$ cannot prove it. So $T 
vdash 
eg G$.

Rosser's improvement replaces "I am not provable" by "for any proof of me there is a shorter proof of my negation", which lets the second half go through using only consistency.

blocks.title: The computability view
blocks.body:
There is a second route to incompleteness through the halting problem: there is no algorithm that decides, given a program $M$, whether $M$ halts on empty input. For each $M$ there is an arithmetic sentence $H_M$ that is true in $\mathbb N$ exactly when $M$ halts (it says "there is a number coding a finished computation of $M$"), and if $M$ does halt, $Q$ proves $H_M$, by checking the computation.

Now suppose $T$ were sound, effectively axiomatised and complete. Given $M$, list all theorems of $T$ (possible because $T$ is effectively axiomatised: run through all strings and check which code proofs) until either $H_M$ or $\neg H_M$ appears. Completeness guarantees that one of them appears, and soundness that the answer is right. That would decide the halting problem, which is impossible. So $T$ is incomplete. This argument also shows that the set of sentences true in $\mathbb N$ is not effectively axiomatisable, and indeed is not even computably enumerable.

blocks.title: Second incompleteness theorem
blocks.body: Let $T$ be a consistent, effectively axiomatised theory extending PA, and let $\mathrm{Con}_T$ be the sentence $\neg \mathrm{Prov}_T(\ulcorner 0 = S0 \urcorner)$. Then $T \nvdash \mathrm{Con}_T$.

blocks.title: Proof sketch
blocks.body:
The first half of the proof of the first theorem showed: if $T$ is consistent, then $T \nvdash G$, so $G$ is true. That reasoning uses only elementary facts about proofs and codes, and it can be carried out inside $T$ itself (PA is strong enough; one checks the Hilbert–Bernays derivability conditions, such as $T \vdash \mathrm{Prov}_T(\ulcorner\alpha\urcorner) \to \mathrm{Prov}_T(\ulcorner \mathrm{Prov}_T(\ulcorner\alpha\urcorner) \urcorner)$). The formalised result is
$$T \vdash \mathrm{Con}_T \to G.$$
If $T$ proved $\mathrm{Con}_T$, modus ponens would give $T \vdash G$, which the first theorem rules out. So $T \nvdash \mathrm{Con}_T$.

blocks.title: What the theorems do and do not say
blocks.body:
They do not say that some statement is unprovable in every system: $T + G$ proves $G$. But $T + G$ is again consistent and effectively axiomatised, so it has its own undecided sentence; the incompleteness cannot be repaired by adding axioms one at a time, or by any effective scheme.

They need all their hypotheses. The theory of all sentences true in $\mathbb N$ is complete and consistent, but not effectively axiomatised. Presburger arithmetic (only $+$, no $\cdot$) and the theory of real closed fields (Tarski) are complete and effectively axiomatised; they are too weak to represent all computable relations.

The second theorem does not show that PA is inconsistent; it shows its consistency cannot be proved by means formalisable in PA. Gentzen (1936) proved the consistency of PA using induction along the ordinal $\varepsilon_0$, a principle outside PA (see [[ordinals-cardinals]]).

Natural undecided statements exist. Goodstein's theorem (every Goodstein sequence reaches 0) is true but not provable in PA (Kirby and Paris, 1982), as is a strengthened finite Ramsey theorem (Paris and Harrington, 1977). In set theory, the continuum hypothesis is neither provable nor refutable in ZFC, assuming ZFC is consistent. And by the work of Matiyasevich, Robinson, Davis and Putnam, for any $T$ as above there is a polynomial Diophantine equation with no solutions in natural numbers for which $T$ cannot prove that it has none.

blocks.title: Computing a Gödel number
blocks.body: Code the symbols by $0 \mapsto 1$, $S \mapsto 2$, $= \ \mapsto 3$. Find the Gödel number of the string $S0 = S0$, and recover the string from its number.
blocks.solution:
The symbol codes are $2, 1, 3, 2, 1$, so the Gödel number is
$$2^2 \cdot 3^1 \cdot 5^3 \cdot 7^2 \cdot 11^1 = 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 125 \cdot 49 \cdot 11 = 808500.$$
To decode, factor: $808500 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5^3 \cdot 7^2 \cdot 11$. The exponents of the successive primes $2, 3, 5, 7, 11$ are $2, 1, 3, 2, 1$, giving back $S, 0, =, S, 0$. Unique factorisation guarantees this always works, provided every symbol code is at least 1, so that no exponent is 0 and the length of the string can be read off.

blocks.title: Goodstein sequences
blocks.body: Write $n$ in hereditary base 2 (write $n$ in base 2, then write each exponent in base 2, and so on). Replace every 2 by 3 and subtract 1. Write the result in hereditary base 3, replace every 3 by 4 and subtract 1, and so on. Compute the sequence starting at 3, and the first few terms starting at 4.
blocks.solution:
Start with 3. In base 2, $3 = 2 + 1$. Replace 2 by 3: $3 + 1 = 4$; subtract 1: $3$. In base 3, $3 = 3^1$; replace 3 by 4 and subtract 1: $4 - 1 = 3$. In base 4, $3$ is a single digit, so the bump changes nothing and we get $2$, then $1$, then $0$. The sequence is $3, 3, 3, 2, 1, 0$.

Start with 4. In hereditary base 2, $4 = 2^2$; replacing 2 by 3 gives $3^3 = 27$, minus 1 is $26 = 2 \cdot 3^2 + 2 \cdot 3 + 2$. Bump to base 4: $2 \cdot 16 + 2 \cdot 4 + 2 = 42$, minus 1 is $41$. Continuing gives $4, 26, 41, 60, 83, 109, 139, 173, \dots$, which grows for an astronomically long time, yet eventually reaches 0. Goodstein proved that every such sequence reaches 0 by attaching to each term an ordinal below $\varepsilon_0$ (replace the base by $\omega$) and noting that these ordinals strictly decrease, which cannot go on forever. Kirby and Paris showed that PA cannot prove this.

blocks.title: Complete theories are decidable
blocks.body: Let $T$ be consistent, complete and effectively axiomatised. Show that there is an algorithm deciding, for each sentence $\sigma$, whether $T \vdash \sigma$. Conclude that any consistent, effectively axiomatised $T$ extending $Q$ in which the set of theorems is undecidable must be incomplete.
blocks.solution:
Since $T$ is effectively axiomatised, we can list all finite strings and test each one to see whether it codes a deduction from $T$, so we can list all theorems of $T$. Given $\sigma$, run this list until $\sigma$ or $\neg\sigma$ appears. By completeness one of them does, so the search stops; by consistency only one of them is ever a theorem. Answer "yes" if $\sigma$ appeared, "no" otherwise.

So for consistent, effectively axiomatised theories, completeness implies that the set of theorems is decidable. But every consistent theory extending $Q$ has an undecidable set of theorems (this essential undecidability of $Q$ goes back to Church and to Tarski, Mostowski and Robinson), so a consistent, effectively axiomatised $T$ extending $Q$ cannot be complete. This is one more proof of the first incompleteness theorem, in Rosser's strong form.

blocks.body:
- Confusing truth with provability. $G$ is true in $\mathbb N$ but not provable in $T$; in some other (nonstandard) models of $T$, $G$ is false, which is why the [[completeness-theorem]] is not contradicted.
- Over-reading. The theorems do not say that mathematics is inconsistent, that minds outperform machines, or that every theory is incomplete; they apply to consistent, effectively axiomatised theories that interpret enough arithmetic.
- Adding the Gödel sentence as an axiom does not produce a complete theory.
- The second theorem is about the specific sentence $\mathrm{Con}_T$ built from a standard provability formula; with deliberately perverse codings of "consistency" it can fail, which is why the derivability conditions matter.
- Weak systems are not automatically incomplete: Presburger arithmetic is complete.

Incompleteness sits between logic and computation. The diagonal argument is the one behind Cantor's theorem in [[ordinals-cardinals]] and the halting problem in [[computability]], and Gentzen's consistency proof measures the strength of PA by the ordinal $\varepsilon_0$. The completeness and compactness theorems of [[completeness-theorem]] explain why unprovable sentences must fail in some model. The negative solution of Hilbert's tenth problem ties incompleteness to [[diophantine]] equations, and the Paris–Harrington theorem shows a statement of [[ramsey]] theory that is true but unprovable in PA. Open problems such as the [[rh]] or [[goldbach]] could in principle be undecidable in a given axiom system, although there is no evidence that they are.

1. With the coding of the first example, which string has Gödel number $2^2 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5 \cdot 7^3 \cdot 11^2 \cdot 13$?
2. Explain why the sentence $G$ of the first theorem is equivalent in $T$ to $\mathrm{Con}_T$ when $T$ extends PA. (Use the second theorem's proof and the fact that an inconsistent theory proves everything.)
3. Show that $T = \mathrm{PA} + \neg \mathrm{Con}_{\mathrm{PA}}$ is consistent if PA is, even though it asserts that PA is inconsistent. Is $T$ sound?
4. Compute the Goodstein sequence starting at 2.
